title: Removal of the GOES 0.7 flux factor in December 2019 explains the Cycle 25 M-flare excess per F10.7 unit and made SWPC M-flare forecasts too low in 2020-2024 (NOAA data 1998-2026)
abstract: Question: how much of the high Solar Cycle 25 flare rate comes from the December 2019 change of the NOAA GOES X-ray flux scale, and did the SWPC flare forecasts follow this change? Method: we matched 34,845 SWPC operational flare events to NCEI science-quality GOES peaks (GOES-8 to GOES-19). We made one homogeneous flare list for 1998-2026. We compared flare rates of Cycles 23, 24 and 25 at matched F10.7, sunspot number and sunspot area with Poisson spline models and 27-day block bootstrap intervals. We verified 9,515 SWPC day-1 to day-3 M-class and X-class probabilities against outcomes on the operational and legacy scales. Results: the science/operational peak ratio steps from 1.451 to 1.016 when GOES-16 became primary in December 2019. Rescaling increases Cycle 24 M-flare counts by 1.53. The Cycle 25/Cycle 24 M-flare rate ratio at matched F10.7 is 1.38 (95% CI 1.10-1.77) with the operational list and 0.92 (0.74-1.15) on one scale. Per sunspot, it falls from 2.21 to 1.45 (1.14-1.84); the remaining excess agrees with about 7-10% more F10.7 per sunspot in Cycle 25. SWPC M-class forecasts were too high in Cycles 23 and 24 (observed/forecast 0.79, 0.78) and too low in Cycle 25 (1.12). The change, 1.43 (1.28-1.59), equals the removed factor; on the legacy scale it is 1.12 (0.99-1.26). Forecasts became higher in 2025-2026 (ratio 0.93), which agrees with an adjustment, but the cycle phase can also explain it. Limitations: three cycles, an incomplete Cycle 25, one constant cycle factor per model, and different answers for different activity indices.
